summary: SSO token refresh triggers header rewrite at edge, clearing model pin during weighted canary
description:
Issue summary:
Customer observed that long-lived sessions which had been pinned to a specific model version during a weighted canary lost their pin after an SSO token refresh flow. The traffic then routed to fallback variants and caused mixed responses across previously stable sessions.

Impact:
- Several enterprise customers (Synthicor Health) reported inconsistent model outputs for ongoing chat sessions during a scheduled canary.
- User sessions that relied on deterministic behavior for clinical prompt evaluation saw divergent results.
- No full outage, but regression in response consistency potentially affecting downstream decision logic.

Environment:
- Production, us-west primary edge; us-east failover.
- Customer using SAML SSO with short-lived session tokens and an auth refresh proxy in front of Redwood edge.
- Canary configuration: weighted rollout of rw-alpha-13b-v1 -> rw-alpha-13b-quantized-v1 at 10% weight.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start a session with tenant X that is pinned to rw-alpha-13b-v1 (long-lived chat, keep-alive idle ~25m).
2. Trigger token refresh by simulating SSO re-auth within the client (refresh endpoint invoked, new Authorization header issued).
3. Observe outgoing requests at our edge for the same session: header sequence is rewritten by the auth proxy (adds X-SSO-Context and rotates Authorization).
4. After the refresh, session affinity appears to be lost: subsequent requests are routed to a canary variant or fallback model.

Observed logs/metrics:
- Edge access logs show session cookie and tenant-id preserved, but pin header (X-Model-Pin) absent for requests immediately after auth refresh.
- Routing service trace shows fallback path triggered: commit decision fell back to routing policy when pin metadata was absent.
- No 5xx errors; increase in 200 responses from canary model with different output signature.

Initial customer hypothesis:
- The auth refresh path strips or rewrites pin-specific headers during token exchange, causing the routing layer to treat the request as stateless and re-evaluate weights.

Notes on urgency:
- Customer is enterprise and flagged as potential compliance risk due to non-deterministic results in production. SLA: P1/Sev1 response required.

investigation_notes:
Technical findings:
- Edge header merge logic treats Authorization changes as a potential identity boundary and clears several ephemeral headers to avoid token leakage across forwarded requests. This logic did not exclude pin-related headers (X-Model-Pin, X-Tenant-Pin).
- SSO token refresh flow uses a 307 redirect and an auth-proxy that performs a header rewrite which triggers edge header-merge path.
- When pin header is removed, the routing layer falls back to weight evaluation and may route to canary or fallback variants.
- Reproduction achieved in staging by simulating SSO redirect + header rewrite; adding passthrough exceptions for X-Model-Pin preserves pin and prevents fallback routing.

Next steps:
1) Create a minimal edge-proxy patch to whitelist model pin headers during header-merge. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/2891)
2) Add an automated unit test to prevent future regressions when auth flow paths are updated.
3) Prepare a targeted canary deploy of the patch in us-west with monitoring on routing divergence metrics.
4) Notify affected enterprise customers and recommend auth-proxy configuration changes as temporary workaround.
resolution: Workaround and fix plan in place: customer applied temporary mitigation to suppress header rewrite for pin headers and confirmed improvement. Edge-proxy patch to whitelist pin headers created and under review. Planned staged deploy with monitoring; post-deploy will verify no regression in header-sanitization safety checks. Follow-up: add test coverage and update runbook to include SSO redirect pattern guidance.
